opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there's a big gap right now between those two regimes. On one end you have pre-training, where the model absorbs an enormous amount of knowledge, but it's slow, expensive, and happens once. On the other end you have in-context learning, which is fast and flexible but ephemeral: once the context window is gone, whatever the model figured out is gone too. Humans have something in between. We learn on the job, we consolidate experiences, we get better at a particular task over weeks and months, and that knowledge sticks.

So I'd expect some kind of middle ground to become important. One version is just longer context and better use of it, where the model can keep notes, retrieve from its own past work, and build up a scratchpad of what it's learned about a project. That's the cheapest thing to do and it'll probably go a long way. But I suspect at some point you want something more like online fine-tuning or memory consolidation, where the model actually updates its weights, or some parameter-efficient piece of its weights, based on what it's experienced during deployment. That's closer to what people do when they sleep on a problem and wake up understanding it better.

There are real challenges there. You have to worry about catastrophic forgetting, about the model learning the wrong lessons from noisy feedback, and about safety, since a model that changes itself while deployed is harder to evaluate than a fixed artifact. But I think the payoff is large, because a lot of valuable work isn't about knowing general facts. It's about accumulating context on a specific codebase, a specific organization, a specific research problem. Right now models start fresh every time, and that's a big limitation.

I'd also add that RL plays a role here. A lot of what makes someone good at a job isn't declarative knowledge, it's procedural: knowing how to recover from mistakes, how to break down a problem, when to ask for help. You get that from practice with feedback, not from reading. So I think the combination of long-horizon RL, some form of persistent memory, and maybe lightweight continual training is what gets you systems that actually improve with experience the way people do.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning from experience and RL practice, but does not propose developing knowledge through the system’s own reasoning.

r002.rationale: It does not describe a system inspecting what it knows to identify what it needs to learn.

r003.rationale: It calls the space between pre-training and in-context learning a “big gap” and proposes a middle ground, but does not identify that space as underexplored.

r004.rationale: It says longer context could help; it does not say expanding context windows reduce incentives to explore other learning methods.

r005.rationale: The response contrasts in-context learning with persistent updates, but does not clearly suggest that fine-tuning and in-context learning provide complementary capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a gap right now between the two mechanisms we have. On one end you've got pretraining, where you're absorbing basically everything humanity has written, but it's frozen at some cutoff and it's extremely sample-inefficient. On the other end you've got in-context learning, which is really fast and flexible, but it's ephemeral. The model learns something during an episode, and then the context is gone and it's back to square one. There's nothing in between that looks like what a person does, where you learn something on Monday and you still know it on Friday, and you've integrated it with everything else you know.

So the thing I'm most interested in is some form of continual learning. The model should be able to take experience, whether that's reading a document, having a conversation, trying something and seeing it fail, and actually update on it in a durable way. Right now the way people approximate this is retrieval, where you store stuff externally and pull it back into context. That works okay, but it's kind of a hack. The model doesn't really "know" the retrieved thing the way it knows facts from pretraining. It can't reason fluently with it, it can't notice when the retrieved thing contradicts something else it believes.

I think the harder and more interesting version is where the weights themselves update, or something functionally equivalent. And the obstacles there are the classic ones. Catastrophic forgetting, where you learn the new thing and clobber old things. And then there's the question of what you should update on at all. Humans are pretty good at deciding what's worth remembering. If I tell you a random phone number, you forget it, but if I tell you something surprising about how the world works, you remember that. So there's a filtering problem that's kind of a metacognitive skill.

The other piece I'd emphasize is that knowledge acquisition shouldn't be passive. A lot of what I'd want from a system is for it to figure out what it doesn't know and go find out. That's where RL comes in naturally. You can set up environments where the model has to actually gather information, run experiments, ask questions, and gets rewarded for being calibrated and for resolving its own uncertainty. I think that kind of active learning is closer to how expertise actually develops. You don't become an expert by reading, you become one by doing and getting feedback and noticing where your model of the world was wrong.

So if I had to summarize, I'd say we need to close the loop. Pretraining gives you the prior, in-context learning gives you fast adaptation, and the missing piece is a mechanism that consolidates experience back into the model over time, ideally driven by the model's own sense of what it's uncertain about.

r001.rationale: The response proposes learning from experience and actively gathering information, but does not say systems develop new knowledge through their own reasoning.

r002.rationale: It says the model should figure out what it does not know and learn based on its own uncertainty.

r003.rationale: It describes pretraining and in-context learning as two existing mechanisms with a missing continual-learning mechanism between them.

r004.rationale: It does not attribute reduced exploration of intermediate learning methods to expanding context windows.

r005.rationale: It contrasts pretraining with in-context learning but does not identify fine-tuning and in-context learning as complementary capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a missing piece around continual learning. During training, the model accumulates knowledge in its weights. And then, at inference time, it can learn things in context, but that learning is temporary. It doesn’t necessarily carry over to the next task.

You’d like a system that can work on a problem, figure something out, and retain something useful from that experience. Not just remember the answer, but improve the way it approaches similar problems. If it spends a long time debugging a piece of code, for example, you’d want it to get better at debugging.

That could involve updating the weights, or it could involve an external memory that the model learns to use. I’m not sure what the right combination is. But storing everything isn’t enough—you need some way to decide what’s worth retaining, whether it’s actually correct, and when it applies. I think that’s a pretty important direction if we want systems that keep improving as they do useful work.

r001.rationale: It proposes that a system work on a problem, figure something out, and retain useful learning from that experience.

r002.rationale: It discusses deciding what to retain, but does not describe introspecting on its own knowledge to identify what it needs to learn.

r003.rationale: It calls continual learning a missing piece and contrasts lasting knowledge in weights with temporary in-context learning.

r004.rationale: It does not connect expanding context windows to reduced incentive to explore learning methods.

r005.rationale: It contrasts training and in-context learning but does not say fine-tuning and in-context learning provide complementary capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a missing piece around continual learning. Right now, we mostly have this separation between training, where the model acquires knowledge, and deployment, where it can use its context but doesn’t really change in a lasting way.

You’d like a system that can work on a problem, discover something, and then retain that discovery so it helps with future problems. Some of that could happen through external memory—writing things down and retrieving them later—and some could happen through updates to the model itself.

The tricky part is deciding what should become durable knowledge. An experience might teach you a general lesson, or it might be misleading. So I think you need a process for testing and consolidating what the system learns, rather than just updating on everything it encounters.

r001.rationale: It proposes that a system work on a problem and discover something it can retain for future problems.

r002.rationale: It discusses testing and consolidating learning, but does not describe introspecting its knowledge to identify what it needs to learn.

r003.rationale: It calls continual learning a missing piece between training and deployment, where the model can use context but does not change durably.

r004.rationale: It does not connect expanding context windows to reduced incentives to explore learning methods.

r005.rationale: It mentions context use and model updates, but does not say fine-tuning and in-context learning provide complementary capabilities.
